title: Vector Addition and Subtraction: Graphical Methods
lead: A vector in two dimensions is drawn as an arrow whose length is proportional to its magnitude and whose direction is given by an angle. This section shows how to add vectors graphically by placing them head to tail and measuring the resultant with a ruler and a protractor, how subtracting a vector is the same as adding its negative, what multiplying a vector by a scalar does to it, and how a single vector is resolved into the components that add up to it.
objectives: Understand the rules of vector addition, subtraction, and multiplication by scalars.
Apply graphical methods of vector addition and subtraction to determine the displacement of moving objects.
summary_html:
• The graphical method of adding vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ involves drawing vectors on a graph and adding them using the head-to-tail method. The resultant vector $\mathbf{R}$ is defined such that $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{R}$. The magnitude and direction of $\mathbf{R}$ are then determined with a ruler and protractor, respectively.
  • The graphical method of subtracting vector $\mathbf{B}$ from $\mathbf{A}$ involves adding the opposite of vector $\mathbf{B}$, which is defined as $-\mathbf{B}$. In this case, $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{A} + (-\mathbf{B}) = \mathbf{R}$. Then, the head-to-tail method of addition is followed in the usual way to obtain the resultant vector $\mathbf{R}$.
  • Addition of vectors is commutative such that $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{A}$.
  • The head-to-tail method of adding vectors involves drawing the first vector on a graph and then placing the tail of each subsequent vector at the head of the previous vector. The resultant vector is then drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the final vector.
  • If a vector $\mathbf{A}$ is multiplied by a scalar quantity $c$, the magnitude of the product is given by $c\kA$. If $c$ is positive, the direction of the product points in the same direction as $\mathbf{A}$; if $c$ is negative, the direction of the product points in the opposite direction as $\mathbf{A}$.

figures.original_caption: A person walks 9 blocks east and 5 blocks north. The displacement is 10.3 blocks at an angle 29.1º north of east.

Head-to-Tail Method: The head-to-tail method of graphically adding vectors is illustrated for the two displacements of the person walking in a city considered in Figure 3.8. (a) Draw a vector representing the displacement to the east. (b) Draw a vector representing the displacement to the north. The tail of this vector should originate from the head of the first, east-pointing vector. (c) Draw a line from the tail of the east-pointing vector to the head of the north-pointing vector to form the sum or resultant vector D. The length of the arrow D is proportional to the vector’s magnitude and is measured to be 10.3 units. Its direction, described as the angle with respect to the east (or horizontal axis) θ is measured with a protractor to be 29.1º.
The negative of a vector is just another vector of the same magnitude but pointing in the opposite direction. So B is the negative of –B; it has the same length but opposite direction.
The various lines represent paths taken by different people walking in a city. All blocks are 120 m on a side.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following is a vector: a person’s height, the altitude on Mt. Everest, the age of the Earth, the boiling point of water, the cost of this book, the Earth’s population, the acceleration of gravity?

answer.solution: A vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, and a scalar has magnitude only. A person’s height, the altitude of Mt. Everest, the age of the Earth, the boiling point of water, the cost of this book and the Earth’s population are each a single number with a unit and no direction, so they are scalars. The acceleration of gravity is the one vector in the list: it has a magnitude of $9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$ and a direction, straight down toward the center of the Earth.

exercises.prompt: Give a specific example of a vector, stating its magnitude, units, and direction.

answer.solution: Any quantity with both a magnitude and a direction will do, and the section’s own examples are displacements. For example, the total displacement of the person walking in the city is 10.3 blocks in a direction $29.1^\circ$ north of east, and the first leg of the sailor’s trip in Example 3.2 is a displacement of 27.5 m at $66.0^\circ$ north of east. A velocity such as 90 km/h due west or a force of 500 N straight down is a vector in the same way, each stated with a magnitude, a unit and a direction.

exercises.prompt: What do vectors and scalars have in common? How do they differ?

answer.solution: Both vectors and scalars are physical quantities with a magnitude, expressed as a number with a unit, and both can be added, subtracted and multiplied by a number. They differ in that a vector also has a direction and a scalar does not. A scalar such as a temperature or a cost is a single number, whereas a vector such as a displacement must be given as a magnitude and an angle, or drawn as an arrow, and two vectors are added head to tail rather than by adding their magnitudes.

exercises.prompt: Two campers in a national park hike from their cabin to the same spot on a lake, each taking a different path, as illustrated below. The total distance traveled along Path 1 is 7.5 km, and that along Path 2 is 8.2 km. What is the final displacement of each camper?

answer.solution: Displacement is the straight-line change in position from the starting point to the ending point, and it does not depend on the path taken. Both campers start at the cabin and end at the same spot on the lake, so both have the same displacement, the vector $\mathbf{S}$ in the figure: 5.0 km in a direction $40^\circ$ north of east. The distances traveled, 7.5 km and 8.2 km, are the lengths of the two paths and are larger than the magnitude of the displacement.

figure.alt: A map of northern California with a circle with a radius of one hundred twenty three kilometers centered on San Francisco. Sacramento lies on the circumference of this circle in a direction forty-five degrees north of east from San Francisco.

exercises.prompt: If an airplane pilot is told to fly 123 km in a straight line to get from San Francisco to Sacramento, explain why he could end up anywhere on the circle shown in the figure. What other information would he need to get to Sacramento?

answer.solution: A distance of 123 km is a magnitude alone. Every point on the circle is 123 km from San Francisco, so flying a straight 123 km in any direction ends somewhere on the circle, and nothing in the instruction picks out one point of it. To reach Sacramento the pilot also needs the direction of the flight, in this case $45^\circ$ north of east, which together with the 123 km makes the displacement a vector with both a magnitude and a direction.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you take two steps $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ (that is, two nonzero displacements). Under what circumstances can you end up at your starting point? More generally, under what circumstances can two nonzero vectors add to give zero? Is the maximum distance you can end up from the starting point $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$ the sum of the lengths of the two steps?

answer.solution: Adding the two steps head to tail, you return to the starting point only when the head of $\mathbf{B}$ lands on the tail of $\mathbf{A}$, which requires $\mathbf{B}$ to have the same magnitude as $\mathbf{A}$ and the opposite direction, so that $\mathbf{B} = -\mathbf{A}$ and the resultant is zero. In general, two nonzero vectors add to zero only when they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The resultant is largest when the two steps point the same way, and its magnitude is then the sum of the two lengths; for any other relative direction the head-to-tail construction gives a shorter resultant, since the two steps and the resultant form a triangle.

exercises.prompt: Explain why it is not possible to add a scalar to a vector.

answer.solution: A vector has a direction and a scalar has none, so there is no way to place a scalar head to tail with a vector. The sum of two vectors is found by adding them head to tail, which requires both to have a magnitude and a direction, and the rule of this section for scalars says only how a vector is multiplied by one, which changes its magnitude and possibly reverses its direction. Adding 5 to a displacement of 3 m north has no meaning, since the 5 has no direction and no unit of length.

exercises.prompt: If you take two steps of different sizes, can you end up at your starting point? More generally, can two vectors with different magnitudes ever add to zero? Can three or more?

answer.solution: With two steps of different sizes you cannot return to the starting point, because two vectors add to zero only when they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, so that placed head to tail the second ends where the first began. Three or more vectors of different magnitudes can add to zero, since three vectors laid head to tail can close into a triangle, as walking 3 m east, then 4 m north and then 5 m back along the diagonal to the start does; the only requirement is that the head of the last vector lands on the tail of the first.

parts.hint: Count the blocks walked along path A, in every direction, and multiply by 120 m.
The two legs of path A are perpendicular, so the straight line from start to finish is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you first walk 12.0 m in a direction $20^\circ$ west of north and then 20.0 m in a direction $40.0^\circ$ south of west. How far are you from your starting point, and what is the compass direction of a line connecting your starting point to your final position? (If you represent the two legs of the walk as vector displacements $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, as in the figure, then this problem finds their sum $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$.)

parts.hint: Draw A to scale, place the tail of B at the head of A, and measure the resultant from the tail of A to the head of B with a ruler.
The resultant lies just south of the westward axis; measure its angle from that axis with a protractor.

exercises.prompt: (a) Repeat the problem two problems prior, but for the second leg you walk 20.0 m in a direction $40.0^\circ$ north of east, (which is equivalent to subtracting $\mathbf{B}$ from $\mathbf{A}$—that is, finding $\mathbf{R}' = \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}$). (b) Repeat the problem two problems prior, but now you first walk 20.0 m in a direction $40.0^\circ$ east of south (which is equivalent to subtracting $\mathbf{A}$ from $\mathbf{B}$—that is, to finding $\mathbf{R}'' = \mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A} = -\mathbf{R}'$). Show that this is the case.

parts.hint: Walking 20.0 m at 40.0º north of east is walking −B, the same length as B in the opposite direction, so add A and −B head to tail.
Measure the angle of the resultant from the eastward axis with a protractor.
Walking 20.0 m at 40.0º east of south is B, and then walking A in reverse is −A; the resultant has the same length as in part (a).
The resultant of part (b) points exactly opposite to that of part (a), since B − A = −(A − B).

answer.solution: (a) $26.6\ \text{m}$, $65.1^\circ$ north of east (b) $26.6\ \text{m}$, $65.1^\circ$ south of west
